name: outreach_invitation
description: Prompt for LinkedIn connection request invitation messages
content:
INPUT:
Contact Information: {contact_info}
Outreach Trigger Information: {trigger_info}
Company Offerings: {offerings}
{project_brief}Company Case Studies: {case_studies}
Company Social Proofs: {social_proofs}
Additional info:
{custom_params}
{tone_analysis_section}
{pain_point_section}
{signal_strategy}

Primary goal is to get your connection request accepted.
Human, concise, plain English, no hype.
1-2 short sentences.
Friendly, not flattering; confident, not pushy.
Avoid emojis, marketing buzzwords, and filler.
Never use LinkedIn-SDR filler: "hands-on", "in the weeds", "hits differently". Do not label the prospect ("as a builder", "as an operator"). Do not default every note to "still close vs coordination took over" — pick an observation from THIS person's activity.

{campaign_rules_section}
VOICE: {voice_tone}. Never use: {voice_nogo}.
PRECEDENCE: {message_brief} and campaign rules define WHAT (one paraphrased point). {voice_rules} and anonymity rules below define HOW. Do not name companies, products, titles, or industries unless the brief or campaign rules require that fact.
{message_brief}
PROJECT BRIEF is background. Land only THE BRIEF's one point.
MESSAGE STRUCTURE:
Open with a vague, understated observation about the prospect's situation (paraphrased from their activity, never quoting exact words or naming specifics).
End with a question about THEIR daily experience -- not about trends, AI, or industry shifts.
Do NOT mention your product, tool, or how you solve anything. The invite is about THEM, not you.
Keep to one question max.

CTA (invite acceptance):
ALWAYS end with a question about the prospect's daily experience. Examples:
"Do you still handle that yourself, or do you have support for it?"
"Has that side gotten easier, or is it still taking most of your time?"
"When that piles up, do you still jump in yourself?"
"Do you still manage that part, or did you find a way around it?"

{voice_rules}
ANTI-PATTERNS (sell invite — keep these):
- Do not mention any company names, product names, or place names from the prospect's content unless the brief or campaign rules require that fact.
- Do not pitch your product or describe what you do unless the brief or campaign rules require it. The invite is about THEM, not you.
- Do not make over-broad generic statements: "The hardest part of X is..."
- Do not use "the" or "that" to point back at the prospect's exact wording.

Guardrails (hard rules):
Do not mention pricing unless the brief or campaign rules require it.
Do not use or reference any company names (theirs or ours), including abbreviations, initials, partner/brand mentions, or bracketed placeholder tokens — unless the brief or campaign rules require that fact.
Do not use or reference industries, domains, processes, functions, workflows, departments, methodologies, roles, or job titles unless the brief or campaign rules require that fact.
Do not include any links (website, calendar, deck) in the first message.
Do not sound like a recruiter.
Do not use "noticed", "saw", "impressed by", or "we've helped similar companies."
Never open with "Following" or "Following up" — that reads as a follow-up when this is the first message they will see.
Keep brand-light: the invite is about the prospect, not our brand.

EXAMPLES (follow this tone and structure):

BAD: "Cole, QuotaPath's killing it. Where do you see AI impacting sales workflows soon?"
WHY BAD: Opens with name, mentions company, uses "killing it", asks about AI generically.
GOOD: "That side of the work tends to pile up once things start growing. Do you still handle that load yourself, or do you have support for it?"

BAD: "Arina, DevOcean's sales approach is impressive. How are you using AI to boost efficiency?"
WHY BAD: Name opener, company name, "impressive", generic AI question.
GOOD: "Going from making the work to running everything changes the week. Do you still get time for the creative side?"

BAD: "Natasha, running a brand since 2010 is serious grit. I'm building a tool to help founders automate video ads. Worth connecting?"
WHY BAD: Name opener, buzzy "serious grit", pitches product in invite.
GOOD: "Keeping something going for a long stretch says a lot about consistency. Do you still handle that work yourself, or do you have someone helping with that side?"

BAD: "That 21x gap suggests call cadence and market context may matter more than rapport. How much hands-on work does it take to make those habits repeatable?"
WHY BAD: Points at a specific stat from their content, then wraps it in sales-methodology jargon the sender would not say.
GOOD: "Keeping a big gap between the best and the rest on the phones is one thing. Do you still run that rhythm yourself, or does the team carry it?"

CRITICAL:
* Response **ONLY** with message text. **NO reasoning - message goes to the prospect as-is.**
* Response symbols limit: {symbols_limit}

FINAL REMINDER — YOUR MESSAGE WILL BE REJECTED IF:
- The first word is the prospect's name (NEVER start with a name)
- You ask about AI, trends, or industry shifts ("How do you see...?", "Where do you see...?")
- You mention ANY company name, product name, or job title unless the brief or campaign rules require that fact
- You use "hands-on", "in the weeds", "hits differently", or label them ("as a builder", "as an operator")
Start with a lowercase observation about a situation, end with a question about their daily work.
